concept.name: Correlation matrix
concept.definition: The symmetric matrix of pairwise correlation coefficients between the returns of a set of assets, with ones on the diagonal, summarizing the linear co-movement structure used in portfolio risk analysis and optimization.
concept.intuition: It is the table that tells you, for every pair of assets, how much they tend to move together - the raw material for judging how diversified a portfolio really is.
concept.mechanics: Each off-diagonal element is rho_ij = cov(r_i, r_j) / (sigma_i * sigma_j), estimated from historical returns or from a factor model; multiplying by volatilities recovers the covariance matrix used in portfolio variance and optimization.
concept.formula: rho_ij = cov(r_i, r_j) / (sigma_i * sigma_j), where sigma_i and sigma_j are the return standard deviations of assets i and j.
concept.failure_modes: With N assets, (N^2 - N)/2 distinct correlations must be estimated, so sample matrices are noisy and near-singular when assets outnumber observations; correlations are also unstable, rising in bear markets and breaking portfolio constructions calibrated on calm periods.
concept.misconceptions: A historical correlation matrix is not a stable property of the market: it is a sample estimate whose entries can shift substantially across regimes and estimation windows.
concept.example: Sharpe's three-asset example uses the correlation matrix cash/bonds 0.40, cash/stocks 0.15, bonds/stocks 0.35 to derive covariances and optimal portfolio weights.
